source_read: PDF (version of record, open access CC BY), General Hospital Psychiatry 74 (2022) 22-31, all ten pages read (pp. 22-31, including funding, conflict statement and references). Text extracted with pdftotext -layout into my own folder and checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Table 1 (pp. 25-26) checked on the rendered pages; Figs 2-4 read from the embedded figure images at their native 300 ppi (forest-plot values legible). Supplement (Tables S1-S3, Figs S1-S3) not in the file and not read.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the panic finding: 'increases' rests on the within-person, blinded placebo comparison (121 of 237 after caffeine, no panic attack after placebo in any study; 8 of 10 studies randomized the order), not on the pooled ratio, and the claim limits it to the doses, setting and medication-free state studied. Slight understatement on anxiety: the claim says only 2 studies reported placebo anxiety data, which matches the abstract and Results 3.5.1, 1st paragraph, but the same section also says 3 studies gave change data for both conditions and that all 5 studies that compared caffeine with placebo statistically found a larger anxiety rise after caffeine, the 4 of them with controls a larger rise in panic disorder (p. 26). The cups conversion is labelled as the authors' equivalence and reads as a description of study conditions, not advice.
claims.note: All numbers recomputed: 121/237 = 51.05%; 69/128 = 53.9%; 2/115 = 1.74%; risk difference 52.2 points; 52/109 = 47.7%; the Table 1 counts sum to these totals when Klein et al.'s group is 5 of 7 (printed 5/17). exp(3.47) = 32.1, exp(2.06) = 7.85, exp(4.87) = 130.3. From the Table 1 counts of the six two-group studies, a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel risk ratio without continuity correction is 32.03 (log 3.467) with a Greenland-Robins log-scale 95% CI of 2.06 to 4.87, which reproduces the text exactly; Fig. 4 prints 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23) with chi-square(5) = 1.58 and I2 = 0% against the text's Q(5) = 8.45, so 'two incompatible pooled risk ratios' is right. Anxiety: from the Fig. 3 study values (SE from each 95% CI), DerSimonian-Laird with Hartung-Knapp intervals reproduces the printed 1.02 (0.08 to 1.96) and, without Nardi et al. 2009 (ref 38, g 2.51, the study the funnel plot flags), gives 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37), as the claim says; a plain z-interval would give 0.25 to 1.19, so the claim's interval follows the method the printed interval implies. Cups: 400/100 = 4 and 750/100 = 7.5. '8 of the 10 come from two research groups' is not stated by the review but follows from its reference list: Uhde is an author of refs 34, 51, 53 and 60 and Nardi first author of refs 38-41 (pp. 30-31); the other two are Charney 1985 and Masdrakis 2015, which also give the 1985-2015 range. One unresolved point: 'about 750 mg' is the review's conversion of Charney et al.'s 10 mg/kg at 75 kg (p. 25), but Table 1 describes that preparation as caffeine citrate (p. 25) and the review does not say whether 10 mg/kg refers to caffeine or to the salt (caffeine citrate is about half caffeine by weight). If it is the salt, that study gave about 375 mg of caffeine, which would change the 400 to 750 mg range and 'no study tested less than 400 mg'; only the primary paper can settle it.

anchors.extracted: 1893 articles identified, 10 included. 9 studies of panic attacks with 237 patients: 51.1% had a panic attack after caffeine, none after placebo. 6 of these compared 128 patients with 115 healthy controls: 53.9% against 1.7%, log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06-4.87). Anxiety: 6 studies, 121 patients and 111 controls, Hedges' g = 1.02 (95% CI 0.09-1.96). Caffeine 400-750 mg; only 3 studies did not use 480 mg, so no dose-response analysis.

Only 2 of the 10 studies reported anxiety data for placebo, so caffeine and placebo could not be compared meta-analytically; the restricted dose range prevented dose-response assessment. Doses described as roughly equivalent to 5 cups of coffee; little is known about doses smaller than 480 mg.

RCTs and controlled clinical trials in adults (18 or older) with a clinician-verified panic disorder diagnosis (DSM-III, DSM-IV, DSM-5, ICD-9 or ICD-10), with or without healthy controls; acute oral or intravenous caffeine against a placebo arm, beverages with identical or as similar as possible flavour; blinded administration required, double blinding and randomized order not required; anxiety and/or panic attacks within 24 h; laboratory or clinical settings; English-language original articles.

All 10 within-subject (caffeine and placebo to everyone); 8 randomized order, 2 fixed with caffeine last; patients blinded in all. 244 patients with panic disorder (outpatient clinics in 9 studies, not reported in 1) and 122 healthy controls; 3 studies without controls. All oral: capsules 2, instant coffee 5, other liquids 3; fixed 480 mg in 7, 400 mg in 1, 10 and 7 mg/kg in 2 (750 and 525 mg at 75 kg). Participants rested; no other tasks. Effects measured 30 to 240 min after intake. Text says nine studies measured anxiety and eight panic attacks (Table 1 shows the reverse).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (rows on p. 25, Uhde controls and footnotes on p. 26)
anchors.extracted: Panic attacks after caffeine, panic disorder and controls: Charney 15/21 and 0/17 (caffeine citrate 10 mg/kg in ginger ale, fixed order, caffeine last); Klein 5 of 7 (printed '5/17 (71%)', n = 7; fixed order, caffeine last); Masdrakis 9/19 (no controls); Nardi ref 39 17/29 and 2/28; Nardi ref 40 38/83 (no controls); Nardi ref 41 13/25 and 0/22; Nardi ref 38 17/28 and 0/26; Newman no panic data; Tancer 3/11 and 0/11; Uhde 4/14 and 0/11. Footnote 2: no panic attacks after placebo. Editors' sums: 121/237 overall; 69/128 against 2/115 in the six two-group studies; 52/109 in the three without controls.

Only 2 studies reported placebo-condition anxiety data (refs 11, 51), so the meta-analysis used caffeine conditions only; 2 studies gave caffeine last. 6 studies, 121 patients and 111 controls: anxiety rose after caffeine in patients, g = 1.94 (95% CI 1.19-2.69), and controls, g = 0.91 (0.46-1.36); greater rise in patients, g = 1.02 (0.09-1.96); Q = 15.0, p = 0.01, I2 = 66.8% (20.7%-86.1%).

Only 3 studies gave change data for both caffeine and placebo (the 1st paragraph says 2); all 5 studies that compared caffeine and placebo statistically found a larger anxiety rise after caffeine, and all 4 of those with controls found larger effects in panic disorder; the remaining 3 studies said placebo did not alter anxiety, without a comparison.

Baseline-post correlation assumed r = 0.5; r = 0.1-0.9 gave similar results. Charney's 30-min value used (90 min similar); Tancer's 90-min STAI used (150-min Zung similar), although Tancer reported a larger rise in patients than controls only at 150 min.

SMD (95% CI): Charney 1985 0.70 (-0.12; 1.52); Nardi 2007a 1.20 (0.52; 1.88); Nardi 2008 0.17 (-0.66; 1.00); Nardi 2009 2.51 (1.50; 3.51); Newman 1992 1.58 (-0.40; 3.56); Tancer 1995 0.23 (-0.99; 1.46); total 1.02 (0.09; 1.96); prediction interval -1.27 to 3.32; chi-square(5) = 15.04, P = .01, I2 = 67%. Editors' recalculation without Nardi 2009 (DerSimonian-Laird, Hartung-Knapp): 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37).

Panic attacks after caffeine and placebo reported in 9 studies (237 patients) and 6 studies (115 controls). Fixed-effects Mantel-Haenszel analysis, said to use continuity correction, of the 6 two-group studies (128 patients, 115 controls): log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06-4.87), Q(5) = 8.45, p = 0.133; 69 patients (53.9%) and 2 controls (1.7%) had a panic attack after caffeine. In the 3 studies without controls 52 of 109 (47.7%). Overall 121 (51.1%) patients and 2 (1.7%) controls; no study reported a panic attack after placebo. Editors' calculation: RR about 32 (7.8 to 130); difference 52.2 points.

Risk ratios with 95% CI by random-effects Mantel-Haenszel; because no panic attack followed placebo and controls had attacks in only one study, 0.5 was added to each cell for individual studies, but the overall RR was computed without continuity correction (contrast Results 3.5.2: fixed effects, with continuity correction). Hedges' g with random effects for anxiety.

anchors.extracted: Funnel plot flagged one study (ref 38) with an unusually large effect on anxiety, a potential bias; no small-study bias seen for panic attacks.

anchors.locator: Discussion 4.1 Summary of evidence, 1st paragraph (begins p. 27) and 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Challenges of 400-750 mg discriminate panic disorder from controls for panic attacks; roughly half of patients and under 2% of controls had a panic attack after caffeine, none after placebo; most studies used 480 mg, called roughly equivalent to 5 cups of coffee. Lack of placebo anxiety data precludes definitive caffeine-placebo conclusions; the anxiogenic effect and patients' greater sensitivity are less certain than the panicogenic effect.
The large doses used (5 cups of coffee) do not reflect an everyday serving, about 100 mg in a brewed cup of coffee; how people with panic disorder respond to small-to-moderate doses is unknown.
All caffeine challenge studies in panic disorder to date assessed anxiety and panic attacks at rest, and all were conducted during abstinence from psychotropic treatment.

Small number of studies; anxiety effects rest on an imputed correlation (robust in sensitivity analyses); instant-coffee doses potentially inexact; whether effects reproduce within the same person on repeat challenge is unknown.

Included studies: Charney 1985 (ref 11); Klein, ..., Uhde 1991 (34); Nardi 2009 (38), 2007 (39), 2007 (40), 2008 (41); Tancer, Stein, Uhde 1995 (51); Uhde 1992 (53); Masdrakis 2015 (59); Newman, ..., Uhde 1992 (60). Years 1985-2015; Uhde an author of four studies and Nardi first author of four (editors' reading of the author lists).

reporting_issues.note: Reproduced: the text's value is a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel RR without continuity correction (32.03, log 3.467, CI 2.06-4.87). Fig. 4's study ratios match a 0.5 continuity correction approximately (Nardi ref 39 8.21 exactly; Charney 25.36 by my calculation against 25.23 printed), and an inverse-variance pooled RR with continuity correction gives about 11.9, close to but not exactly 12.12, so the figure's exact method cannot be identified.
Table 1 shows panic counts for 9 studies (Newman none) and anxiety entries for 8 (Masdrakis and Nardi ref 40 blank); Results 3.2.4 (p. 25) says nine anxiety and eight panic.
All three typesetting errors are on p. 25 (Charney, Klein and Masdrakis rows), not pp. 25-27.
The text gives Q, p and I2 with its interval (p. 26) but never the prediction interval, which is only in Fig. 3 (p. 27).
Methods 2.7 lists and counts six domains (p. 24); Fig. 2 has seven rows, adding other sources of bias; the panic counts on p. 27 cite Fig. 2 where Fig. 4 is meant.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low follows from items 4, 11 and 13, each defensibly not met. Item 15 'yes' is generous (funnel plots with 6 studies; the flagged study was not followed up by a sensitivity analysis), but the overall rating does not change.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the counts support the abstract's panic conclusion; the gaps are the abstract's choice of one of two incompatible pooled ratios and its unqualified statement that caffeine increases anxiety, which the discussion itself grades as less certain.

missed: Dose of Charney et al. (1985): Table 1 calls it caffeine citrate 10 mg/kg (p. 25), while the text converts 10 mg/kg into about 750 mg of caffeine at 75 kg (p. 25). The review does not say whether the dose is expressed as caffeine or as the citrate salt (about half caffeine by weight); if the salt, that study's caffeine dose would be near 375 mg, which would change the 400-750 mg range and the statement that no study tested less than 400 mg. Needs the primary paper.
Fig. 2 shows blinding of participants and personnel unclear in about a fifth of studies, while Results 3.2.1 says patients were blinded in all studies (p. 25).
The pooled anxiety analysis uses Tancer et al.'s 90-min STAI value (g 0.23 in Fig. 3), although Tancer reported a larger rise in panic disorder than in controls only at 150 min (p. 26).
